title: WHAT IF YOU COULD SEE HOW MUCH MONEY EVERYONE HAS?

segments.line: You are standing in the lunch line when it happens. Above the
cashier's head, a number appears.
Forty dollars. It floats there soft and white like a price tag in the air.
Nobody else looks up. Nobody else can see it. You
blink, the number stays. Mrs.
Park hands you your tray and takes your lunch money. Her number
ticks up. Forty dollars. Forty-four dollars. Forty-eight dollars.
Money just moved and you watched it move. Sam
elbows you in the ribs. You okay? You look like you saw a
ghost. You
point up. Above her head, the number. Sam
looks. What number? And that's when you
get it. The numbers are
only for you. So
what if you could see how much money everyone has? Here's the
deal. You figure out three rules fast.
Rule one, the number is everything a person has.
Cash in a wallet, money in the bank. All of it
added up floating over their head. Rule
two, it ticks. The
second money moves, the number moves. Money in, it
flashes green and climbs. Money out, it flashes red and
drops. Rule
three, you can't see your own number. You stand in front of the bathroom
mirror and look up.
Nothing. No number above your head at all.
File that away. You'll need it. You
test rule two that night at home. Your mom pays the
electric bill on her phone. One tap. Her number drops one
hundred and twelve dollars in a single blink. You test it on Sam the next
morning. He buys a
snack. His number drops two dollars and fifty cents. Sam grins. The
emergency five stays in the shoe, though. That's the
rule, so you run an
experiment. All day at school, you read everyone. Mrs.
Hale, your teacher, twelve thousand, four hundred dollars. She buys two
coffees every morning, one for her. One she leaves on the
janitor's cart,
Maya, the quiet girl, three hundred and twelve dollars. She
draws in a notebook all through lunch. She shares her
fries with anyone who sits down.
Sam, two hundred and twelve dollars and fifty cents. He
saves every lunch dollar. The emergency five stays in the
shoe. The principal, Mr.
Grant, eighty-six thousand dollars. He eats lunch
alone in his office, door closed. At the snack
machine, a kid feeds in two dollars. His number ticks
down, two dollars, right in front of you. You could
watch anyone's money move any time you wanted. It feels like a
superpower. It feels a little bit like
spying. Then
Derek, the captain. New
shoes every week, his dad's car in the parking lot.
Everybody wants to be Derek, his number,
zero dollars. zero. not one dollar. You
stare so long he notices, what are you
looking at? Nothing, you say,
nice shoes. And in the
hallway between classes, you see something else. A man
mopping the floor. Above his head, a number so big it doesn't fit your
brain.
eight million, four hundred and twelve thousand, and nine dollars. You
blink, he turns the corner. Gone, you tell yourself you
imagined it. Nobody has that
kind of money and mops a school hallway. This next bit is
real. No one can
actually see a number above your head. That's the made up part. But the part about money and
happiness, scientists tested that. In twenty-ten, two researchers named
Kahneman and Deaton studied thousands of Americans. They found something
strange. Happiness
climbs as income climbs up to about seventy-five thousand dollars a year. Then it
stops. More money after that doesn't make people feel
better day to day. The number keeps
growing. The feeling doesn't. And in two thousand eight, three more researchers,
Dunn, Aknin, and Norton, ran a different test. They
gave people money and told half of them to spend it on themselves and half to spend it on
someone else. The people who spent it on someone else felt
happier. Every time, so the
science says two things. Money
helps up to a point and
giving it away feels better than keeping it. But the numbers above everyone's heads don't
show any of that. They only show the
money. And that's when the numbers start to
cost you. Because
knowing someone's number feels like power. And power is
hard to put down. At lunch, Derek is
showing off his new shoes again. The whole
table is watching and you say it. Out
loud in front of everyone. Nice shoes, Derek. Too
bad you've got zero dollars. The table goes
quiet, then it laughs. Derek's face goes
red, he stands up. He walks out, Sam looks at you like you just
kicked a dog. That was
mean, you didn't have to say it. You feel
powerful for about two seconds, then you feel sick. Because the number was
true and it still hurt. And it doesn't
stop there, first it's small. You
bet Sam five dollars that the new kid has less than a hundred. You
win. It feels clever, then it's
bigger. You start
checking numbers before you talk to anyone, like a price tag on a person. You
catch yourself checking Maya's three hundred dollars before you
decide where to sit. You sit with the
big numbers, you avoid the small ones. You
notice yourself doing it, you don't stop. That
night you stand in front of the bathroom mirror again,
still nothing above your head. You
ask Sam the next day, what do you think mine says? Sam
shrugs, I can't see any numbers. Only you can, and it
hits you. You spent a whole week
ranking everyone and you don't even know your own
rank, but here's the
worse part. Mrs. Hale's
twelve thousand doesn't say she's kind. Maya's three hundred doesn't say she's
generous. Derek's
zero doesn't say he's a bad person. The numbers
told you about money. You
decided they meant worth, so after
school you go back to the hallway. Mr.
Ellis is there, the janitor.
Mopping the same floor he's mopped for forty years. Above his head, eight million four hundred and twelve thousand and
nine dollars. The
richest person in the whole school, you were
right. You didn't imagine it, he
finishes mopping. He picks up the coffee Mrs. Hale left on his cart. He
smiles at it like it's a gift. You
walk up to him, Mr. Ellis. Why do you still work here? He
leans on his mop. Somebody's got to keep the floors clean, and the kids are good company. Here's what the number doesn't
say,
forty years of saving. A small
inheritance from his mother that he never touched, it
grew year after year while he just kept mopping. He has
millions, and he mops floors because he likes it here. And Derek, the one everyone
envies. He has zero dollars because he
spends everything the
second he gets it, trying to look rich. The numbers were right all
along. Your
reading of them was wrong. The
next morning you walk into school, and the numbers are still there. But this time you look at
faces first. You sit with Maya. She
shares her fries. You
apologize to Derek. He nods and that's enough. At
lunch, Sam does something. He
takes the emergency five out of his shoe, the five he
swore he'd never spend and buys Derek lunch. Emergency, he says. This
counts, Derek
eats. Nobody laughs. That feels better than any number. Sam is
already saving up a new emergency five. He doesn't even care. On your way out, you
pass Mr. Ellis still mopping. His
number is still there.
Eight million four hundred and twelve thousand and nine dollars. You don't even
read it anymore. You just say
morning Mr. Ellis. He says morning
kid. And that's the whole thing. And you
finally get it. The number never
measures what a person is worth. It
never did.
If you could see one number above everyone's head, what would you want it to be? What would
yours say? Tell us in the comments.
